opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The basic worry is this: right now, almost everyone shares in the wealth of civilization because they have something to offer. You have your labor, and your ability to think and produce things. Even the most powerful institutions, whether states, corporations, or militaries, need lots of people to cooperate with them. That dependence quietly gives ordinary people a lot of bargaining power. It's a big part of why states invest in education, healthcare, and infrastructure for their citizens. A productive, healthy population is how a state gets tax revenue, an economy, and an army.

Once AI can substitute for human labor across the board, and not just for particular tasks, that dependence starts to go away. A company doesn't need to hire you. A government doesn't need your tax dollars, because most of its revenue might come from AI-run firms. It doesn't need you to staff its bureaucracy or its military either. So the structural reasons these institutions have to care about you get weaker.

People often reply, "Well, we'll just redistribute. We'll have a UBI, we'll tax the AI companies." Maybe. But that means your income now depends on political goodwill rather than on anything you can withhold. Historically, groups that have nothing the powerful need don't tend to do well over the long run. Think of resource-rich states that don't need their citizens' labor. They often end up less accountable to their populations.

What worries me most is that this doesn't require anyone to be evil, and it doesn't require a dramatic takeover. It can happen gradually through competition. Firms that replace humans with AI outcompete firms that don't. States that let AI-driven growth run most efficiently outcompete states that put human welfare first. Each step looks locally reasonable, and maybe even good, since things get cheaper and GDP goes up. But humans as a whole could end up with a shrinking share of the economy and less ability to steer it, even while the absolute amount of wealth grows enormously.

So I don't think "AI makes the pie bigger, so everyone gets more" is a safe assumption. It depends on humans keeping some real leverage over how the pie gets divided, and that leverage is exactly what's at risk.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention private ownership of AI companies or barriers to ordinary people investing in them.

r002.rationale: It says exclusion can happen gradually through competition, without anyone needing to be evil or stage a dramatic takeover.

r003.rationale: It does not say wealth-creating AIs will have incentives to concentrate enrichment in small, local circles.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the basic worry is that right now, humans are economically relevant almost by default. If you want anything done — building things, running a company, doing research, even just caring for people — you need humans to do it. And that need is what gives ordinary people leverage. It's why wages are high, it's why governments bother to be responsive to their citizens, it's why institutions have to at least pretend to care about what people want. A lot of the nice things about the modern world aren't really the result of anyone being especially benevolent; they're the result of people being useful and therefore having bargaining power.

The thing that changes with sufficiently advanced AI is that this usefulness could just go away. If AIs can do essentially every job better and cheaper than a person, then from the point of view of a company or a state, humans stop being an input to production and become more like a cost. You don't need their labour, and so you don't need to pay them, and you don't need to listen to them. The wealth is still being created — possibly vastly more of it than ever before — but the mechanism that used to channel some of it to regular people was that they contributed to making it. Once that contribution is zero, there's no automatic reason the flow continues.

People sometimes respond, "well, we'll just redistribute it — universal basic income, taxes on capital, whatever." And I think that's possible, but I want to flag how much it depends on political power that people may no longer have. Historically, when a group loses economic relevance, their political relevance tends to erode too, sometimes slowly, sometimes not. If the people and organizations who actually control the AI systems don't need the rest of us for anything — not for labour, not for soldiers, not for consumption in any meaningful sense — then redistribution becomes something that happens purely out of goodwill or inertia. And I'm just not confident that goodwill and inertia are stable foundations over decades.

So it's not a story about AI being malicious, or even about a dramatic takeover. It's a more gradual, almost boring story: the deals that currently hold society together quietly stop making sense for the powerful parties, and nobody has to do anything villainous for humans to end up on the outside of where the value is being generated. That's what I mean by "excluded." It's less like being robbed and more like being left behind by an economy that no longer has a slot for you.

r001.rationale: The response discusses people losing economic and political leverage, but does not mention private ownership of AI companies or barriers to investing in them.

r002.rationale: It says humans could be left outside the value being generated without anyone acting villainously, and that the deals holding society together could quietly stop making sense.

r003.rationale: It describes wealth and control resting with AI operators, but does not say that AIs have incentives to concentrate enrichment in small, localized circles.

astra-6.text:
Well, right now, most people get a share of the economy’s output because they have something to sell: their labour. If AI can do essentially everything that a person can do, more cheaply, then that mechanism stops working. The economy could be growing enormously while the value of human labour falls towards zero.

You might say, “But surely everything will become cheaper, so everyone will benefit.” And cheaper goods would help. But that doesn’t guarantee you an income, or a claim on things that remain scarce, like land. If you don’t own any of the capital producing this wealth, it’s not clear why you’d receive a share of it.

There’s also a political concern. Workers have bargaining power partly because society needs their participation. If the people who own the AI systems no longer need everyone else’s labour, that source of bargaining power weakens.

So I don’t think exclusion is inevitable. We could arrange broad ownership or redistribute the proceeds. But those are choices we’d have to make. Making society much richer doesn’t, by itself, ensure that everyone shares in that wealth.

r001.rationale: The response discusses lacking ownership of AI-producing capital, but does not identify private ownership of major AI companies as a barrier to investing directly in them.

r002.rationale: It describes how people could lose income and bargaining power, but does not state that institutions can exclude most people without anyone deliberately arranging it.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute incentives to wealth-creating AIs or say they would concentrate enrichment within small, localized circles.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, right now, most people get a share of the economy’s output because they have something valuable to contribute: their labor. Even if you don’t own a lot of capital, you can earn money by doing something that somebody else needs done. But if AI can do essentially all of those things more cheaply, that mechanism stops working. The economy could become enormously productive while most people have very little claim on what it produces.

And I think it’s easy to conflate two things: humans no longer needing to work, and humans being able to afford not to work. The first doesn’t automatically give you the second. If you own the AI systems, or other assets that remain valuable, you might do extremely well. If all you have to sell is your labor, you could lose your bargaining power.

Now, we could choose to distribute that wealth broadly. But that requires some institutional mechanism; it isn’t something that follows automatically from making the technology more capable. And we’d want to establish that while people still have the economic and political power to demand it.

r001.rationale: The response says AI owners may benefit, but does not identify private ownership of major AI companies as a barrier to ordinary people investing directly in them.

r002.rationale: It says broad distribution requires an institutional mechanism and is not automatic, but does not state that institutions can exclude most people without anyone deliberately arranging it.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe wealth-creating AIs as having incentives to enrich small, localized circles.
